title: Direct pressure and the bleeding ladder
hook:
A cook has slipped with a knife and opened a deep cut on his forearm. Dark red blood flows steadily onto the floor. His coworker has already pressed three paper towels onto it and is about to peel them off to see how it looks.

Most external bleeding stops with one thing done well: firm pressure, held, and left alone. This lesson is how to do that, and how to tell when it is not enough.

steps.find: You look at the blood: bright red and spurting, dark red and flowing steadily, or a dark ooze.
steps.act: That tells you the vessel. Arterial bleeding (bright red, spurting with the pulse) is the hardest to control and the fastest to kill; venous bleeding flows steadily; capillary bleeding oozes and often stops on its own.

steps.find: The bleeding is severe or spurting and you have no dressing in your hand.
steps.act: Put a gloved hand straight on the wound. Do not spend time looking for a dressing first.

steps.find: Your hand or a dressing is on the wound.
steps.act: Press firmly, toward a bone where there is one, and hold it. For massive bleeding, hold pressure all the way to the hospital; for lesser bleeding, it is reasonable to check after 5 to 10 minutes.

steps.find: Blood is soaking through what you placed.
steps.act: Do not lift it off and do not pile on more gauze. Leave it, and escalate: wound packing with a hemostatic agent, or a tourniquet for a wound on a limb.
Convert to a pressure dressing: bandage the dressing firmly so the pressure holds without your hands, and keep checking for bleed-through.

ideas: Pressure works by squeezing the tissue around the wound, slowing the flow through the damaged vessels and giving the body time to clot.
Never remove a dressing once it is placed. Lifting it tears away the clot forming under it.
Too much gauze is a mistake. Layers soak up blood without stopping it and cushion your hand away from the wound.
Volume depends on size. An adult holds about 5 liters of blood. A sudden loss of about 1 liter is serious in an adult, about 500 mL in a child and 100 to 200 mL in an infant.
Life-threatening bleeding from a limb does not climb this ladder: it gets a tourniquet straight away (the next lesson).
Nosebleeds are managed by sitting the patient up, leaning forward, and pinching the soft part of the nostrils. Leaning back sends blood into the stomach and causes vomiting.

misconception.wrong: When a dressing soaks through, take it off and put on a fresh, dry one so you can see the wound.
misconception.right: A soaked dressing stays where it is. Taking it off disrupts the clot. Bleed-through is the signal to escalate to packing with a hemostatic agent or, on a limb, a tourniquet.

check.q: Blood is bright red and spurting from a wound in time with the patient's pulse. Which vessel is most likely open?
options: A capillary bed
A large vein
An artery
A small vein
check.why: Arterial blood is bright red because it is fully oxygenated, and it spurts because it is under the pressure the heart generates. It is the hardest bleeding to control and the fastest to kill.

check.q: You have held firm pressure on a leg wound, and blood is now soaking through the gauze. What is the next step?
options: Remove the gauze and apply a fresh dressing
Leave the gauze and escalate the bleeding control
Add several more layers of gauze on top
Elevate the leg and loosen your grip slightly
check.why: Never remove a placed dressing, and piling on gauze weakens your pressure. Bleed-through means escalate: wound packing with a hemostatic agent or, on a limb, a tourniquet.

check.q: A patient has a steady nosebleed that started on its own. How should you position them?
options: Sitting up, leaning forward, pinching the soft part of the nose
Lying flat on the back with the legs raised
Sitting up with the head tilted back
Lying on the side with the head lower than the feet
check.why: Upright, leaning forward, with the soft part of the nostrils pinched. Tilting the head back sends the blood down the throat into the stomach, which causes vomiting.

check.q: Which sudden blood loss is serious for a child, according to the usual rule of thumb?
options: About 50 mL
About 1.5 liters
About 100 mL
About 500 mL
check.why: A sudden loss of about 500 mL is serious in a child, about 1 liter in an adult, and as little as 100 to 200 mL in an infant.

check.q: A patient's forearm is bleeding heavily and you have no dressing in reach. What do you do?
options: Go back to the ambulance for a trauma dressing
Place your gloved hand directly on the wound
Wait for your partner to bring the jump kit
Ask the patient to hold the arm above the head
check.why: For severe or spurting bleeding, a gloved hand goes straight onto the wound. Time spent hunting for a dressing is blood the patient does not get back.

summary: Direct pressure controls most external bleeding: compress the wound (a gloved hand at once if it is severe), hold the pressure, leave what you placed undisturbed, and escalate if it fails. Bleed-through means packing with a hemostatic agent or, on a limb, a tourniquet; it never means removing the dressing. Once bleeding stops, a pressure dressing holds it. Life-threatening limb bleeding skips straight to a tourniquet.
